speechtext: That when this House adjourns on Wednesday, the 23rd inst., it stand adjourned to Tuesday the 29th inst.

Before the motion is carried, may I call the attention of the right hon. First Minister to the fact that, owing to the position in which some of the maritime province members are placed, an adjournment from Wednesday until Tuesday is rather awkward. For myself, going to Prince Edward Island, it means that I have either to lose some days from the House or spend two nights on the road to get into Charlottetown on Saturday at midnight and leave Monday morning. I would like to ask the First Minster if he could not see his way clear to amend the motion so that instead of having the adjournment to Tuesday, it be to the Wednesday following, which would be conferring a great favour upon us, and be most convenient for us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is a matter as to which the government are quite willing to place themselves in the judgment of the House. If it is preferred that we should reconvene on Wednesday, the 30th, instead of Tuesday the 29th, we are quite willing.
Several hon. members from the west have spoken to me on the same subject, and they would prefer Wednesday to Tuesday.

Personally, I am nearing the end of the second session in which I have lost one day. I have not been able to go home at any time except upon the occasion of the last Christmas holidays. I represent in that respect a number of western members who come long distances to serve their country, at a great deal of inconvenience, and if the views of the Prince Edward Islanders are to be met they will be met by keeping other gentlemen here, who cannot go home at all, in absolute idleness.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In order to accommodate both the east and the west we will say Wednesday the 30th.
Motion as amended, agreed to.

Six weeks ago, I questioned the government as to why the new public building in Lachute was not being used as a post office, and on my visit to Lachute a short time ago, I was much surprised to find that the post office was closed yet, so iar as the transaction of business is concerned. The building was practically completed many months ago, the caretaker has been living in it all winter, and it is being heated and lighted at the public expense while the public have not the use of it. The Lachute post office is a distributing centre for many of
the smaller post offices, and it is very much needed. Why has it not been opened for the transaction of business?

I am glad the hon. member has brought this matter to my attention. It may be that the Public Works Department has not yet given the Post Office Department possession, but if it has I will see that the post office is opened at once.
The Minister of Public Works informed me yesterday that the building had been transferred to the Post Office Department.
If that is so the postmaster will be installed immediately.

The building has been placed at the disposal of the Post Office Department, and the postmaster has recently been asking for certain equipment which no doubt will be supplied as sou: as possible. I think my department has done all that is necessary.

TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I ask the Minister of Finance whether it is the intention of the government to make any statement before the adjournment next Wednesday in connection witn the tariff issue between the United States and Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Further amount required for steam service between Canada and Mexico, upon the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, $16,666.66.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: This vote is intended for the service on the Atlantic and the Pacific. Originally the Mexican government paid $50,000 in gold, and Canada a similar amount. The Mexican government ceased paying anything, and the Canadian government, rather than see the service abandoned, granted an additional $25,000 per annum, making $75,000 in all. This amount of $16,666 is to cover that portion of the fiscal year 1909-10, since the Mexican government ceased paying their share of the subsidy.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What business is being done by this line and what are the prospects?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: There is a considerable trade outward, but not very much coming back. That is the reason the Mexican government did not seem disposed to continue their share of the subsidy. From the Canadian point of view, however, the traffic is very encouraging.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
We ought to have a specific statement, giving the exact amount of the trade. Will the minister at the same time give us a statement of how it is divided between the Atlantic and the Pacific?
. Mr. FIELDING. The vote is a general one for tooth the Atlantic and the Pacific, but this increase is entirely for the Pacific side. The full details of the traffic are contained in a departmental report which is now in the printer's hands and will reach hon. -members shortly. The tonnage carried outward during the recent months has been as follows: September, 766 tons weight and measurement; October, 2,228 tons weight, and measurement, November, no sailing, December, 3,133 tons weight, and measurement, January, the figures are not yet available.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: How frequent is the service on the Atlantic and on the Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Monthly on to-oth oceans.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What portion of this belongs to the mail service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The mails are carried on all subsidized steamers as a condition of the contract, but there is no specific allotment for mail purposes.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: -Can the minister state what the amount of subsidy per ton of freight is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: No, we haven't it worked out in that form.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would give us some idea of what the aggregate trade is between Canada and Mexico.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The department report, which has already been presented to the House, contains information of that character. If on examination anything more is required, we shall be happy to supplement it.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Can the minister give us the total increase in the steamship subsidies and subventions this year as compared with last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I haven't it at hand, but I shall be very glad to get it or any other information desired, and endeavour to supply it at another stage of the trade and commerce estimates.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Steam service between Canada and Cuba, $15,000.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Why is this increase, and why did it arise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: This is a new service. The contract was entered into with Messrs. William Thomson & Company, of St. John, at the rate of $25,000 per annum, one sailing per month. This amount of $15,000 is intended to cover the service performed since November last, but all of it may not be required.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
How is it a new
service? The government has not power to enter into a contract without the consent of this House. There must have been an amount voted for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Services of this character are placed under contract with the qualifying condition that no money can be paid until it is appropriated by parliament-. It is not an unusual proceeding.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: It has been done, but it is rather unusual, and it is not the_ correct principle qf carrying on the business of the country.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Perhaps in the main my hon. friend is right. Before a dollar is expended, we should have an appropriation by parliament; but sometimes that is found to interfere with efficient business, and if the parties to a contract are willing to enter into the arrangement on the condition that I have mentioned, I cannot see any objection to it. The failure to do it might prevent the doing of something which parliament would wish to have done as promptly as possible.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I understand that this matter came up last autumn, a demand having been made toy the people of St. John for a line between that city and Cuba. While I have not anything to say against St. John, I wish to point out that the only port in the maritime provinces to which steamers plying between Canada and Cuba will come is the port of Halifax, and they afford sufficient accommodation for all the trade that is carried without any subsidy at all.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What line is that?

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The Pickford & Black Company put on boats whenever they are required.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: They get large subsidies for the West India service.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
They do not get any for Cuba. I do not know whether the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) or the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Eichard Cartwright) was communicated with, but, there must have been some communication from

the port of Halifax in regard to this matter. On account of this subsidy feeing granted, this steamer was brought to St. John and loaded largely with potatoes which she carried to the port of Havana and flooded that market to such an extent that shippers in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick lost a great deal of money. I understand from the statement of the Minister of Finance that all the money will not be required. That means no doubt that the steamship is not going to 'Continue the monthly trip. Is that the case? I have no desire to interfere with the port of St. John or any other port. I desire that every port should be given all the accommodation possible, but I do not think it wise to subsidize one line to compete against others. I shall be glad when the time comes when we shall be able, to dispense with subsidies, but am satisfied in the meantime that such subsidies as are necessary to encourage trade and commerce should be given. I might refer to the Mexican trade as an instance in which a subsidy is very advantageous. But if any fair minded man will consult with the merchants of St. John, he will be told that the subsidy to the line in question was not conducive to their best interests.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: This service established between St. John and Cuba has been of the very greatest possible benefit. If my hon. friend were to communicate with the board of trade and the merchants and shippers of St. John, he would find that the service has been very successful in the way of developing trade, and has given satisfaction to the shippers, not only from St. John, but from up the valley of the St. John river, more especially in the counties of Carleton, Victoria, and other sections. My hon. friend says that the steamship lines from Halifax to Cuba will afford all the accommodation necessary. I am always glad to see trade developed from the port of Halifax, but the difficulty with that port is that it is too far away from the point of production in New Brunswick to be of any advantage to the people producing hay and potatoes and other agricultural products in the valley of the St. John river, one of the best sections in the whole of Canada for the production of potatoes. The only difficulty was the want of a market, but by reason of the establishment of this line, these people have been able to market thehr potatoes in large quantities. These potatoes are a great favourite in the Cuban market, and the result has been an enormous benefit to the farmers of the St. John river valley. As to the line which the Department of Trade and Commerce agreed to subsidize, it was bound to give one sailing per month. As a matter of fact, in the two months, during which its steamers have been running, it has given seven sailings instead of one per month. In one month it gave three sailings instead of one. It did that because of the development of trade and because it was reasonably necessary for the accommodation of the public.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: How many sailings in February and March?

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: March is not much more than half through, but in February, I think they had two sailings.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Does the minister know whether they had any sailings at all or not?

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Yes, I am quite sure they had one, and I think they had two.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Is this steamship service, to which we are paying a subsidy of $25,000 a year, to continue every month in the year?

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: That is the expectation.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I am not asking what is the expectation, but what the contract is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: This contract requires a monthlv service. My hon. friend is mistaken when he says that the service from Halifax is performed without a subsidy. There, is a service subsidized from Halifax to Cuba.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: There is only the Mexican line which calls at Cuba.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: That is a subsidized service.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: But here you have a line subsidized from St. John direct to Cuba and back. The line from Montreal in the summer, and Halifax in the winter, touching at Havana, calls at the Bahama islands and Cuba, and goes down to Mexico. We get all the boats we want in Halifax in ihe season when freights are offering; and if very little freight offers, it is difficult to get boats to carry on the service until next November. Before the government entered into a contract to pay a subsidy of $25,000 to a steamship line between St! John and Cuba, they should have been able to show whether there was any necessity for it or whether that service could not be had without a subsidy. I have no desire to oppose the granting of a subsidy where necessary for the general benefit of Canada, but I am opposed to the granting of subsidies where they are not required. That is why I take exception to this subsidy. People in Halifax were very much disappointed when it was granted, and from the information I have, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) must have had some communication from the merchants in the export trade, indicating that all the accommodation necessary for the trade with Cuba could be had at Halifax without charge to this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: According to my hon. friend, all the accommodation which Halifax desires must be given even with the assistance of subsidies. But the province of New Brunswick is largely engaged in the production of potatoes, and if the trade there wishes to export them to Cuba, I do not see why they should not have the right to do so; and as St. John is more convenient for the shipment of New Brunswick produce, I do not see why the St. John people should not have a line subsidized to Cuba.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: If the Halifax merchants can get all the freight accommodation they want, the St. John people ought to be able to get the same. The boats chartered from Halifax come to that port at a season when freight is offered, so that the trade can get all the accommodation they require. These boats to Cuba will not carry the mails, the mails go by way of New York. They are subsidized from St. John simply for the purpose of carrying freight and nothing else, and are not suitable for carrying the mails any way. I am not asking that Halifax be put on a different footing from St. John, but that it be on an equal basis.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: We have always thought that Halifax was treated better than St. John.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: It is easy to prove that the hon. minister is wrong, and when the time comes, I shall be able to do that. When we take up the railway question I shall be able to show that St. John has a great advantage of one per cent per 100 pounds over Halifax. All we want is to be on a fair and equal basis with St. John, but I do say it is unfair to grant a subsidy to St. John to a boat running in competition with boats that run qn their own bottoms from Halifax, and so put the merchants and exporters of Halifax in a different position from those in St. John. I want them to be on an even basis, and on an even basis we are able to play our part in exporting, or importing at all times. But I do not want to have Halifax placed at a disadvantage by giving $2,000 a month to a boat to run from St. John or any other part of Canada. The Minister of Finance must know this better than I do because he is more familiar with these things. He refers to the steamship company that trades [DOT]between Montreal in summer via Halifax, and the Bahama Islands, and Cuba, and then to Mexico, hut he should know that that service has nothing to do with the direct trade with Cuba.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I do not understand my hon. friend. A vessel sailing from Halifax to Cuba, and landing goods there is in direct trade with Cuba. There is that steamer running direct to Cuba, and enjoying a government subsidy. It is true that Mr. CROSBY.
Halifax has occasional other steamers that do not enjoy a subsidy, but it is also true that both Halifax and St. John have subsidized lines to Cuba.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance surely does not want us to believe that a boat sailing from Montreal, calling at Halifax, and then going to the Bahamas, and calling at Cuba, and on to Mexico, is a direct subsized boat from Halifax to Cuba.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The New Brunswick people have the same right, and opportunity that the people of Halifax, and Nova Scotia have on this line subsized from Montreal in the summer, and from Halifax in the winter to Cuba and Mexico, but here we have a steamship line subsidized last November, a contract made by the government last November, yet no intimation was given to the House last session that such a thing was intended. Now we are asked to vote the money. I think it is quite unfair. The understanding was that nothing was to be paid unless we granted it. It should not be granted because I do not think they are entitled to anvthing. If it was necessary that this should be given in order to facilitate the trade of Canada, and Cuba I would be quite satisfied, but that is not the case, and no one has shown or attempted to show that we have not now all the accommodation required for our trade with Cuba, which is chiefly the fish and potato trade. We have a lumber trade which is carried by sailing vessels, and we have all the accommodation required for that trade. No one in St. John or in Nova Scotia has any desire to have the lumber trade diverted from sailing boats to steamers. The fish and potato trade is all that requires accommodation. I protest against this $25,000 subsidy to a service that is not required.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Will this line running to Cuba also run to Mexico?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: This line to which this item refers does not go to Mexico, but the other line to which I referred, after serving the trade between Halifax and Cuba, proceeds on to Mexico.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I notice that the total amount in the main and supplementary estimates granted to these two lines is something like $65,000 more thi3 year than last year. That is the subsidy to the line running to Mexico is increased this year by $25,000, and the main estimates contain $25,000 for the line to Cuba, which I presume is the same line towards which you are giving the additional $15,000 in the supplementary estimates, making $40,000 of subsidy to that line where last year there was nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
There seems to be a misconception. These is an additional

subsidy of $25,000 for a line from St. John to Cuba. That is a new vote, an addition to the subsidies of last year. The other item shows an increase of $16,000 for the current year on the Pacific side towards Mexico. That is not the Atlantic service at all. On the Pacific we are taking up to some extent the burden which the Mexican government had to lay down.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I may inform the
minister that the potato business, which looms so largely in his mind, last year amounted to $57,000, and he is giving $25,000 to improve that service. The exports to the British West Indies were $2,549,000, whilst the imports were over $7,000,000. Thus the West Indies are getting the benefit of our market through our subsidy. Have the West Indies expressed any desire to add to these subsidies as they benefit by them three times as much as we do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: That is rather a broad question. The subject of trade relations with the West Indies is at this moment engaging the attention of a Royal Commission on which the Minister of Customs has been sitting. I was also a member, but unfortunately was not able to go to the West Indies. The West Indies have not felt able to contribute to these subsidies in the past. The arrangement has hitherto been one sided, both with respect to subsidies, and to the preference. We are trying to bring about a better understanding, how successfully remains to he seen. The West Indies are not too prosperous, and not as well able as Canada to assist commercial enterprise. While it is an undoubted fact that they get advantage of the trade coming this way. it is of considerable advantage to Canada, that we should encourage our export trade to the West Indies. That has been a large trade in bygone years for the lower provinces, and we still hope that it will be a trade that will command the encouragement of parliament.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) should be able to show some reason other than those he has given for the extraordinary contract he has entered into. A contract for which there is no vote of parliament should be justified by some extraordinary reason, something in the nature of an emergency. No such cause as that is alleged. Surely, the New Brunswick trade in potatoes was as great in preceding years as it is now. When such a contract is entered into, for which there is no vote of parliament, there should be some other justification than such a statement as that of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) of the extraordinary quantity of potatoes coming down the St. John river for shipment to Cuba. If there was an extraordinary crop last year, are
the conditions likely to bring about a repetition of that crop next year?

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Then, it is now probably about what it has been for fifty years past, and so the question is one which ought to have been considered by the government before now and ought to have been brought to the attention of the House. What I protest against is this manner of doing business, the government entering into a contract for so important a matter as a subsidy with an ocean steamship company without any authority of parliament and for no better reasons than the carrying of the surplus stock of potatoes from the St. John river to Cuba. The very fact that a commission is sitting for the purpose of inquiring into this matter of West Indian trade is the reason why no such arrangement should^ have been made without consideration of the matter by parliament, unless there was some stronger and more urgent reason than those that have already been stated to us. I enter my protest against such a manner of carrying on the business of the country.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. J. Haggart) says that there must have been the same surplus of potatoes at any time during me last fifty years as last year. I assure my hon. friend that he is entirely mistaken. In the valley of the St. John river, and more especially in the county of Carleton, as my hon. friend from that' county (Mr. Carvell) well knows, a great deal more attention has been paid to the cultivation of potatoes- in recent years than in the past. People have been going into the business scientifically, and it is not unusual for a farmer to raise $4,000 or $5,000 worth of potatoes in a season. Therefore, this is a matter of enormous importance to a great many farmers. About a year ago the Department of Trade and Commerce very wisely sent a trade commissioner to Cuba. That gentleman made a very careful investigation of the Cuban market, and the possibilities of a large business in potatoes and other products of Canada. His reports gave great encouragement as to the possibilities of doing business in potatoes in that market. The farmers of Carleton and other parts of the St. John valley had been finding a market for potatoes in Montreal and Ottawa-they had even sent them as far west as Toronto, but, owing to the freight rates, there was very little profit in the business for the farmer, and some years no profit at all. Therefore, they began to turn their attention to the Cuban market, and especially view of the report of the trade commissioner appointed by this government.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What about the American market from which they were shut out about a year ago?

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: That was also an important fact which necessarily had its influence. Under' the former tariff of the United States the duty upon potatoes was 25 cents per bushel, but by the recent tariff legislation it was increased to 40 cents, a prohibitory rate. Therefore, the farmers were obliged to turn to Cuba for a market, and it did seem as if there were vast possibilities of creating a profitable business there. So strongly did the people feel upon this subject that, last season, the provincial government undertook to assist in the work by renting a warehouse in Cuba and also a warehouse in the city of St. John to facilitate the storage of potatoes until they could be sent forward. My hon. friend from Carleton came to Ottawa in the interest of the people, and as the result of large meetings that had been held in various sections of the county of Carleton, and urged in the strongest possible manner that this government should take steps to procure a regular service between St. John and Cuba, so that the producer might know that there would be an opportunity of sending potatoes forward regularly, and that the Cuban market could be cultivated with a greater degree of certainty. The government, after very careful consideration, yielded to the representations made on behalf of the people who had met to discuss the matter altogether irrespective of politics, and in such large numbers that it was evident that the feeling was universal that here was an opportunity to develop trade which ought not to be missed. The government agreed to give the aid, and, while the company was bound to give a sailing once a month, it has, up to the present time, given two or three sailings a month. The business has developed greatly. My hon. friend from North Sim-coe (Mr. J. A. Currie) speaks of the total value of potatoes sent to Cuba as having been $57,000

The suggestion regarding the making of alcohol from potatoes, is of the highest importance to this country. It comes well within the scope of a national policy. The Minister of Inland Revenue should take up this question of making spirits out of potatoes without putting on a tax. There is a way of doing that so that it will not come into competition with spirits that pay excise duty. Germany has found a way of doing it and that has contributed very largely to her industrial progress. The Germans make spirits out of potatoes which do not come into competition with the spirit that pays excise duty, and as a result Germany has the cheapest alcohol in the world for manufacturing purposes. Germany does not need to import great quantities of gasoline; she is quite independent of the oil combine that exists in the United States and that fixes the price of gasoline the world over. We may have the same condition in Canada if, as these hon. members tell us, the maritime provinces can produce potatoes in such enormous quantities. The need of some kind of spirit in competition with gasoline for industrial purposes is constantly growing.
I venture the prediction that within five years all the agricultural machinery of the northwest will be run either by gasoline or by alcohol. If by gasoline, we shall have to import from the United States; if by alcohol used in engines based onj the principle of explosion, we can produce that alcohol in enormous quantities. In France and Germany every encouragement is given to the cheap production of spirit of this kind. All we have to do is to follow their example. The maritime province members could, not do a better thing than to urge the government to appoint a commission to inquire how this industry may be encouraged. Once it is done, it will be easy to carry it on, seeing that it has been made a success elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext:
It is the easiest thing in the world to manufacture alcohol from potatoes. If the farmers can grow potatoes cheaply enough, the thing is done. If the farmers of Prince Edward Island would prefer to grow potatoes that would net them, probably, 8 cents to 10 cents a bushel instead of the 40 cents to 50 cents i
which they now get, it will be possible to manufacture in Canada alcohol for power purposes. When I say 10 cents a bushel, I am speaking approximately and from what I remember of the figures of two or three years ago when this question was before the House. I have all the data in my office. To get denatured alcohol down in price to compete with gasoline means potatoes at from 10 to 12 cents per bushel. I am aware that a poor class of potatoes produce even a larger quantity of alcohol than potatoes which are better for food. I suppose that is the kind from which alcohol for industrial purposes is made in Germany. But there is no use of comparing Canada with Germany-and Germany is the only place where alcohol for power purposes is made on a large scale from potatoes, for I do not think the manufacture in France is very large. Germany encourages this manufacture by a bounty. In the first place, the government there controls the manufacture of alcohol-I do not understand the system but they control it. And there is a higher tax on alcohol intended to be used as a drink than upon crude alcohol used as an illuminant or for fuel. On the other hand they put a tax upon petroleum, thereby increasing the price when imported into Germany. If we are prepared to do all this in Canada, we may solve the problem of getting the cost of alcohol down to something like 15 or 20 cents per gallon. Two or three years ago, a wave of interest in the question of denatured alcohol arose in the United States and passed into Canada. The United States congress enacted a law giving permission to remove alcohol from bonded warehouses to be denatured and put upon the market for this purpose, and also took power to authorize the establishment of small distilleries on the farms to produce alcohol from cbrnstalks and other rough or waste vegetable matter. To-day. I believe, there is not one of these distilleries in the United States. Even in the corn belt of Illinois, where the cheapest alcohol on this continent can be manufactured, alcohol is taken out of bond and denatured and is put on the market as a fuel and illuminant, if I mistake not, at' about 40 cents per wine gallon, which would be at the rate of about 48 or 50 cents per imperial gallon. It is utter nonsense to talk about manufacturing alcohol in Canada out of potatoes grown for that purpose by the high-priced labour of the farms of this country to compete against the alcohol of the great, corn belt. There is no question of duty at all; we could remit the dutv if the alcohol were, used for industrial purposes, and we do so now'. If the farmers of Prince Edw'ard Island can demonstrate that they can produce potatoes at a price that will permit the manufactured alcohol to be

sold at a less price than gasoline, we will arrange very quickly that they shall have permission for the manufacture. A distillery license costs $250, but that could be removed in the case of industrial alcohol. But from our investigation, we are convinced that alcohol cannot under existing conditions be made in Canada at a rate to compete with gasoline or petroleum. If my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) or anybody else can demonstrate to the Department of Inland Revenue that it can be done, I give my promise that the legislation will be introduced to enable the manufacture of alcohol for industrial purposes to be carried on. It is not a question of legislation but of manufacture.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: When we were discussing the item for dredging a few evenings ago, I drew attention to the need of dredging the port of Weymouth. On.' that occasion I was informed by the minister that the quantity necessary to be removed, according to the plan of the department's engineer, was in the neighbourhood of 500,000 cubic yards. I have been urging the hon. minister to make a beginning at least during this year on this work. I have since had communications from the commercial interests of Weymouth, particularly those pngaged in the shipping interests. They tell me that while they would like the work to be done up to the plans of the department, they recognize the very large demands on the department for the use of their dredges, and the fact that the vote must necessarily be limited in amount. They, therefore, would not ask that the entire work proposed by this plan be done m one year, but they are very anxious indeed that a beginning should be made. At the entrance to the port there is a bar which has been made in tile course of many years, and is a serious obstruction to the Shipping. I am informed by vessel owners and vessel charterers that by a very reasonable amount of dredging, that bar can be cut down sufficiently to admit vessels of a tonnage now unable to get over it, and which the needs of shipping in that locality call for. I am requested to urge on the minister that, in view of the fact that he has increased his vote, enlarged his dredging plant, and that, with the exception of two dredges, it is in very fair condition, he should make a beginning this coming season.

subtopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I would like to go on with the dredging at Weymouth, but my hon. friend will see himself that where there are 500,000 cubic yards to be removed, to really do effective work, work which would be satisfactory and which probably would cost 50 cents per cubic yard-that was the tender price-it is a question for grave consideration as to whether the department would be justified in spending one-quarter of a million dollars to improve the harbour. I have already given the matter consideration, and am not without hope that we may be able in the near future to do some work which may result in improvement, but I cannot say when the work will commence.

I am not asking, nor are the people of Weymouth asking, that this entire 500,000 cubic yards should be removed at this time, but that only a reasonable amount of dredging be done at the entrance to the harbour. The dredging which requires to be done above the bar in the way of straightening the channel might stand for the present. And that, for the time being, can stand. I can assure the minister that, if he will make a beginning, that beginning need not entail a very serious outlay. A comparatively small outlay will improve conditions there wonderfully, and I trust he will not allow The _ plans which have been made, and the estimates of the amount of material to be moved, to frighten him, for we are not asking for that. These plans are very elaborate, and it may be they were made for effect rather than with a view of ever being worked up to, but that they should be held up as a reason why some work should not be undertaken. I do not think that is reasonable or right. We are not asking that the entire plans be worked out, but that a beginning be made, and that the bar at the entrance of the harbour be cut down a reasonable degree so as to allow shipping to pass. I do not think it is fair of the minister to hold up this estimate of 500,000 cubic yards of material to be moved, and a quarter of million dollars spent, when we ask for some dredging. I hope he will not allow that to alarm him out of spending a reasonable amount of money on the entrance to the harbour.

In the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), I desire to support the observations of my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson). We are spending large sums of money for such works as the Transcontinental railway, the Hudson Bay railway and others of that kind. But the people of Weymouth, unfortunately, are not reached by any! of these large works.
And, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in such cases, has used the argument that the people cannot be expected to pay taxes for works from which they benefit only very indirectly unless they receive a -quid pro quo. It is the duty of the government, according to the argument of the Minister of Finance, to see to it that these parties in the maritime provinces, and especially in the port of Weymouth, are recouped for the expenditures they are making in other parts of the -country by an expenditure for works in which they are locally interested and which they demand as a right from the government.

Surveys of Richelieu and Yamaska rivers and their affluents to determine the cost of improved waterways between the river St. Lawrence and Lake Champlain - further amount, $4,000.

The appropriation for this service was $20,000. The actual expenditure was as follows: Salaries of survey party No. 1 to 28th February, 1910, $11,895.11; 'survey party No. 2 $7,447.75: survey party No. 3, $4,333.76; sundries, $ 147.il; total, $23,623.69.
What is the object of the survey?
The object is better water connection between the St. Lawrence and Lake Champlain, and also Lake Champlain and the River Yamaska and some other rivers near the lake.

I thought there might be in view the bigger object of making a connection in the future for the improved St. Lawrence canals or the Georgian Bay canal looking to a deep waterway connection with New York. Unless the service contemplates something of that kind, I do not see the object. We may have, certainly we ought to have, a survey of a 22 foot to a 25 foot canal from the

St. Lawrence down, probably by way oi the route that Young used to advocate from Montreal by way of Lake Cham' plain.
There has been no such survey of recent years; it may have been made a long time ago.
But this one is going on at the present time?
I think it is a very desirable expenditure in the public interest to ascertain the feasibility of getting a deep waterway and the cost.
I want to know if that is what the money is being expended for?
Yes.
Is this for the purpose of carrying the course of the water from the St. Lawrence to Lake Champlain or from Lake Champlain to the St. Lawrence?

Lake Champlain runs to the St. Lawrence. We do not propose to alter the course of the flow of the river; this is only to get a better navigable channel to connect Lake Champlain with the St. Lawrence. There is in connection with that another proposition to cut a channel through from near Montreal across to the Richelieu river which would shorten the distance by about 100 milesi, and make the water route from Montreal to New York a little shorter than the railway haul.

That is the difficulty. [DOT]Who are going to benefit by that, ourselves or the Americans? The whole thing it seems to me would tend towards diverting the trade of the St. Lawrence to New York. Practically all of Lake Champlain is in the United States, so we would facilitate the diversion of trade into the United States, and that seems to me to be a very risky thing for us to do. We have evidence that some of the great steamship lines plying between the old country and New York have been compelled to give up the St. Lawrence, and possibly if they can get the trade diverted, and have it go by Lake Chamolain to New York they will not come up the St. Lawrence.

I do not think the committee will be very much alarmed at any project which may result in giving opportunities for the farmers and producers generally to get their produce to a great city like New York for sale, but we are not proposing anything of that kind, because we are making a survey to see the feasibility of the channel.

Does not my hon. friend see that there is an objection to improving a waterway from Canada to New
York? On general principles that would seem to be objectionable whether foT the benefit of the farmers or of anybody else.
I should think our farmers would be patriotic enough to want to improve our water-waysjor the benefit of Canadian cities; not of the United States cities. The very statement of my hon. friend seems to me to put this item out of consideration by this committee instead of leading us to approve it. He said it would improve the water communication from that part of the country to New York. We have not yet annexed New York. I hope we will do so, I hope the Union Jack will be flying over New York some day, but until we do annex it, I do not think we should spend the money of the people in improving such a waterway.

At the recess we were discussing a small amount required to pay for surveys of the Richelieu and Yam-aska rivers. An appropriation was voted last session, and there is a small amount now due the surveyors.
Was that by the resident engineers?

There was a special survey party made up for this work. It was the work of surveying the Richelieu from its mouth up to its outlet from lake Champlain. And also the Yamaska and tributaries with the view of ascertaining the possibility of connecting those rivers and what it would cost.
Experimental farms and additional branch stations-further amount required, $25,900.

Mr: GEO. TAYLOR. I understand that these items are duplicated in the main estimates not passed. A great many members want to speak on these, and I presume they can do that on the main estimates.
In the main estimates for the ensuing year there will be similar items and ample opportunity for discussion.
Why do you require this additional amount?

With regard to the experimental farm we found that nearly $10,000 had lapsed in last year's vote, and we had to pay out of this year's appropriations. In consequence of the death of Dr. Fletcher, I was obliged to appoint two men, an entymologist and a botanist. They asked for a considerable amount of apparatus, and books, amounting to nearly $5,000. After careful consideration by Dr. Saunders, he recommended that the equipment should be supplied. The result of these two is a deficiency of $15,000. There was an expenditure of $2,000 or $3,000 in preparation for the purpose of some additional branch farms in the west. The money was spent in obtaining information and inspecting sites. Again, I have been doing extra work in connection with tobacco growing which, in the aggregate, has cost $5,000. This accounts for about $23,000, and the balance of $2,000 is for small amounts to close up the business of the year.

The minister says he had to take out of this year's vote to make up for last year's accounts. There is no justification for that. The money voted for this year should not "be used for last year's accounts.
The fact that the Auditor General allows this does not make it right.
But it shows that it is a practice that is followed.

A great many practices have been begun by this government that we think are verv wrong, and this is one of them. I do not think there is any justification for paying money after the vote has lapsed. Money is voted by parliament for a given year, and it is certainly not proper to use the money of one year for the purpose of another.
How many additional experimental farms have been established this year?

One in Prince Edward Island, and one in Rosthern, Saskatchewan. I have had an officer investigating sites that have been suggested in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Quebec and Nova Scotia,
Did the minister establish a farm in any part of western Ontario as he promised last year?

No, and I have none vet in view. I think I said that I hoped to see an experimental farm established in new Ontario. But we hqve not yet reached the point where it seemed well to establish such a farm. I think there ought to be one, perhaps two, experimental farms in the northern part of New Ontario, but it seems better to wait until the construction of the Transcontinental is further advanced, and the course of settlement is moTe clearly decided.
The minister gave us to understand that he would establish an experimental station in western Ontario, not only to assist the tobacco growers-
That is established.
I asked the minister about that.

I did not understand that that was what was referred to. I established a station for experimental tobacco work in Essex county, and also a similar station in Quebec. These account for about $5,000 of expenditure.

I understood that the establishment of a fruit station in western Ontario would be taken up seriously, and I would urge the minister to investigate with that view. I think he is hardly justified in waiting until the Transcontinental line is located before he locates an experimental farm in the northern part of New Ontario. I hope he will look into the matter.
I will do so gladly.

What steps has the minister taken in regard to an experimental station in the semi-arid belt of British Columbia? The statement made by the minister on a previous occasion led the people to hope that a station would be established there this year. Many requests have been made for the establishment of

such a station. I should like very much to have a statement from the minister, and of a favourable character.

I am pushing that as rapidly as possible. I have been waiting for some little information, which I would not like to announce at present, as to a particular site. I have had careful examination made of a number of sites, and have gone over the report of the officer who examined them. In view of this, and some information that I acquired when in that country, I hope before the end of this year that the matter will be settled. I had not intended to go into it on this item; perhaps it woirld be better to leave a fuller explanation until the main estimates are before the committee.

Injustice is often done to inland constituencies in our part of Ontario. A great deal of money is spent by the Dominion for harbour improvements to the benefit of certain ridings, while inland ridings get nothing at all. I have been many years in this House, and have asked for several things, and have failed to get any grant that I ever asked for. East Huron is as good a riding as there is in Canada, and an experimental farm there would yield as good results as in any other place I know of. A great many hundreds of millions of dollars have been voted away since I oame into this House. I have asked once or twice for little things that I wished to have done for East Huron, but no request that I have ever made has been granted. Now I would ask for an experimental fruit farm in East Huron. Because of the peculiar position we occupy-elevation, the proximity of the lake, and the nature of the soil- we have, I believe, the finest apple-growing section in Canada. 1 have heard others claim something of that kind for their localities, but, for a particular kind of apple, the Northern Spy, I think we have the best condition to be found in the country. The Northern Spy ripens in East Huron exactly at the season when nature provides it with all the benefits which in other localities have to be procured by means of artificial cold storage. The farmers there, however, do not know what to do. They do not understand spraying their orchards or how to get rid of the codling moth, and other pests. I am sure that if a small experimental fruit farm were established there-if it were only a farm of ten or fifteen acres-and handled properly, it would mean a great deal to the people of that part of the country. I know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) would like to do what is fair and right, and I would ask him to remember that an inland riding like mine, that has been paying and paying for years, ought Mr. BURRELL.
as a matter of the barest justice, to get something. I would ask the minister to kindly remember that there is an old man up in' East Huron, and that he would like to get something for East Huron before he dies.

I want to assure my hon. friend that I never forget, I shall not say the old man, but my hon. friend, who is so vigorous and young notwithstanding his grey hairs, the representative of East Huron (Mr. T. Chisholm). When the main estimate for the experimental farms for next year comes up, I will be glad to have a very thorough discussion of this whole question of branch farms. I look forward to it with interest, and will be glad to have suggestions such as my hon. friend has made in reference to what I consider a very important branch of the service.
In what position is the farm which the government is establishing in Prince Edward Island?

The farm is in our possession, the buildings are fairly towards completion, and I think the house will be ready for the farm manager before spring. A good deal of fencing was done last fall, the arrangement of the farm is completed, the plots, &c., have been laid out, and a good deal of ploughing has been done, so that I think a large part of the farm will be under cultivation this spring. The farm consists of between 50 and 75 acres just outside of Charlottetown.
Exhibitions-further amount required (including Governor General's warrant for $25,000), $75,000.
How do you come to have a Governor General's warrant?

The decision to exhibit at the Brussels exhibition was not arrived at until after the last session, and in order to move our exhibit from Seattle to Brussels we had to take a Governor General's warrant. Then an additional $50,000 is required because we had expected at the time we took the warrant that parliament would have voted money for this purpose before this, and as the work had to go on we have been obliged to do a good deal of it on credit.
What exhibitions will be participated in this year?

Last summer we were at Seattle. This coming spring the International Exhibition in Brussels opens, and we have arranged for a Canadian pavilion there. Lately we have been invited and strongly urged by a very influential committee in London to take part in what is known as the Festival of Empire at the Crystal Palace, and the government has decided that it would be very unfortunate if at such a celebration as that, Canada was not represented. We are just now taking

the steps necessary to be represented, and that and the Brussels exhibition are the only two I know of in the ensuing year.
