Public works-capital-harbours and rivers -Port Arthur and Fort William-harbour and river improvements, $425,000.
What is the explanation of that very large amount?

This is to cover the following progress estimates, certified to by the chief engineer, for works performed under contracts in force at Port Arthur and Fort William during the fiscal year in excess of those covered by the appropriation of $600,000 which was made by parliament at the session of the year 1908-9; also drawbacks which have been retained on the works and which, of course, have to be paid. First, I will give the different contracts showing the amounts which are due to the different companies. There was a contract dated June 27, 1906, with the Great Lakes Dredging Company for dredging in the Kaministiquia and Mission rivers. For the September account there is $8,964.93; October account, $592.20; November, $1,464. which with a ten per cent drawback amounting to $4,526.17, makes $15,490. 94. Then, there is another contract, dated June 4, 1909, with the same company for dredging on the Kaministiquia and Mission
rivers. That was a contract for additional depth. Hon. gentlemen will remember that at the last session I stated that it was proposed to increase the depth of water there from 22 feet, as had been originally designed, to 25 feet, which seemed to be regarded as necessary to accommodate the larger lake steamers which had recently been built for traffic on the lakes. The September account amounted to $32,714.37; October, $5,925.44; November, $959.42, ten per cent drawback, $16,326.39, making a total of $55,925.63. There was another contract, dated the 27th of February, 1909, for dredging out the terminal basin in connection with the terminals of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. The September account was $48,127.22; October, $116,267.71; November, $102,495.58; December, $26,743.98; ten per cent drawback, $14,049.40, making a total of $307,783.89. There was a contract with Mr. W. J. Hogan for the Port Arthur breakwater. There is a balance due to the 30t-h September of $31,760. Adding that to the previous amount makes the total $410,960.46. Then, there is a contract, dated June 28, with Mr. W. H. Phinn, of Welland, for dredging at Port Arthur. That was dredging that was regarded as urgent in order to give the requisite accommodation at Port Arthur. There is an amount due to Mr. Phinn of $10,263.82 for work done from the 1st October to the 22nd October. That makes the total amount due contractors for works performed in excess of those covered by the appropriation of $600,000 of $421,224.28. In addition to this, there is a progress estimate up to October 30, 1909, of $16,168 for timber supplied for Fort William harbour improvements; that is for revetment wall, which is being constructed along the face of the harbour on the Mission river. This estimate was only received by the accountant on the 16th February, 191u. If I had received that item, I would have had that added to the supplementanes. However, that can be paid out of the main estimates next year. We will still be short about $12,000 for the closing up of these accounts. We have only asked for $425,000, while the total amount is a little over $437,000. We had on hand on the 17th February, to make further payment for timber, land expropriated, engineering expenses and contingencies, $15,335.69. Hon. gentlemen may ask how it was that so much was allowed to be done in excess of the appropriation. The reason is this: At the last session of parliament we cut down the appropriation to the smallest possible figure. I had myself thought that with the appro-, priation which we had it would be impossible to have the work proceed throughout the season as vigorously as it ought to proceed, but my hon. friend the Minister of Finance thought we should curtail, as far as possible, and we did so. Later on in the season, we were pressed very earn-

estly by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to complete the work of dredging up to the very large elevator which the Grand Trunk Pacific is erecting, and after discussing the matter in council, it was decided that it would be wise to allow the contractors to push the work with all possible expedition. The contractors had contracts for the whole work, and it did not make very much difference to the country whether the work was done this year or next year, while the Grand Trunk Pacific represented to us the enormous importance of having a channel dredged through from the Mission river to the pier forming part of the elevator system, either by the 1st of October or very early in October. It was noped by the Grad Trunk Pacific that they would be able to handle the grain of the western country tributary to their railway through the outlet at Fort William.
How much did they handle-one small train load only?

They did not, as it happened, but I felt that as far as my Department was concerned, we ought not to be behind. I gave the assurance to the Grand Trunk Pacific that as far as we were concerned we would do our part.
Are they carrying gram there now?

I do not know. I am bound to say that we did our part, we dredged out the channel so that by the middle of October steamers could go right in through the Mission river and up to the Grand Trunk Pacific elevator.
Was the dredging done by tender?
Yes, the contracts w'ere all given by tender.
At how much?

There were different prices. The contract for the terminal basin was let at sixteen cents. Then, a large portion of the work is being done at eleven cents, and a portion at nine cents. They put on one powerful hydraulic dredge to expedite the work, but most of the dredges are of the ordinary dipper type. We did not contemplate last session that we would have to do any great additional dredging at Port Arthur, but it was brought to our attention that a company was erecting a large grain elevator, and unless dredging was done the lake vessels would not be able to reach it. In view of the fact that at Port Arthur, and Fort William there converges all the grain trade of the west during the season of navigation, and that there was likely to be a large crop, we thought we should provide the necessary facilities. Tenders were invited, and Mr. Phinn, at thirteen cents per cubic yard, Mr. PUGSLEY.
was the lowest tenderer. Mr. Hogan ha3 had for some time a contract for the building of the breakwater at Port Arthur which will form part of the larger harbour improvements which were strongly recommended by the Transportation Commission, and which are essential for the protection of the harbour. We entered into a contract for the building of a revetment wall or system of wharfage along the Mission rivey in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific terminals, and we required the Grand Trunk Pacific to convey to the Crown the title to a thirty foot strip along the harbour front so that it may be open to shipping generally at rates to be controlled by the government. We think it desirable to close up those accounts before the end of the present fiscal year.
The vote in the main estimates last year was $600,000, and with this vote the expenditure will be considerably over $1,000,000 which seems a large sum of money for one particular place.
There are two places, Port Arthur and Fort William.

The vote is under the same head, and it is practically the one city. This expenditure at the one place makes it very diffcult to get grants for necessary public works at other places in the province of Ontario. What will be the total cost of these works?
The total estimated cost, so far as the government is concerned, is in the vicinity of $5,000,000 or $6,000,000.
How much has been already spent?

I should think something over one-half. It must be borne in mind that Port Arthur and Fort William are at the gateway of our great western country which is developing with marvellous rapidity. These two cities are growing at an equally marvellous rate, and the business which has developed there is simply enormous. It is a national port. The improvements at Mission river will extend for six miles along the front and there are industries springing up everywhere. The Grand Trunk Pacific elevator now under construction is to have an initial capacity of 3,000,000 bushels, and their plans contemplate an elevator capacity of 30,000,000 bushels. At Fort William and Port Arthur there is an elevator capacity in the vicinity of 40,000,000 bushels. I believe the Grand Trunk Pacific terminals will be the finest in the world. I do not believe that anywhere in the world will there be a better layout of terminals than in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific, unless it be the terminals of the Canadian Pacific railway, which are also at Fort William. The Canadian Pacific railway have bought considerable property to enlarge their terminals,
and they are taking means to accommodate this vast traffic expeditiously and cheaply.
Enlarging the spout?
It would require as much dredging as if they handled 50,000,000 ' bushels.

Not at all. There was no necessity for bringing in the largest boat for that small amount of grain, and as a matter of fact millions of bushels have been shipped from Port Arthur by vessels drawing less than 18 feet. Could it not have been foreseen that it would be required and submitted to this House? Then the House could have considered it, and would doubtless, if it were needed, have voted the money. But not a word of it was mentioned to the House or the country. We were told that $600,000 was all that would be required for the year, and that was granted without any dissent; and later the government commenced dredging and working on the breakwater and the revetment wall at Port Arthur, all of which the engineer who visited the locality and made his survey must have known and foreseen last year, because the works- there were laid out years ago, and it was well known what improvements would be required from year to year for several years. But in undertaking new work amounting to nearly half a million dollars, and in going on with the expenditure when there was not a dollar voted by parliament for it, the Minister of Public Works has introduced
a very pernicious and improper principle, which parliament should not tolerate. If there had been a storm or an accident^ that necessitated the work being done in a hurry, I could understand the hon. minister resorting to a Governor General's warrant. But these works are not of that character; they were known beforehand, and under these circumstances to expend $425,000 without the consent of parliament is unjustifiable. The minister might just as well have expended as many millions; the principle is the same. I think this is the first Minister of Public Works I have ever known to make such a proposal in this House, and parliament will be doing a very improper thing if it consents to it.
My hon. friend assumes that this work has been paid for. It has not been paid for, and that is the reason we are asking for this vote.
Even if it is not paid for, you have committed the country, and it must be paid for.

I am only correcting a mistake the hon. gentleman made. My hon. friend also says that we have entered on the construction of this breakwater without the consent of parliament. This breakwater has been under construction for three years, and there have been votes for it each year. The contractor is to build the breakwater, and he could go on and finish it in one year if he chose, but he would have to wait for his money until parliament voted it. If a contractor for any work carried it on more rapidly than we anticipated we could force him to wait until parliament voted the necessary money to pay him for the work done. But we thought that was not desirable. . As these contractors, in order to give these much-needed facilities, went on much faster than we had anticipated, we have thought it only right and desirable in the interest of the country that the work of the year should be closed up, and that we should ask parliament for an amount sufficient to close up these accounts before the end of the present month.
How much of this $425,000 represents new contracts entered into by the minister?

The $15,490.94 was under an old contract of June 27, 1906. There is $307,783.89 due under a contract dated February 27, 1909. That was before we had taken our appropriation from parliament. This is practically a part of the original contract. The only difference is that we are digging to a depth of three feet beyond what we had originally intended. But it is all part of the original scheme.
How was it that the minister could not have provided for that last year when he let the contract?

I have already explained that we thought $600,000 would be all we could afford last year; but if the contractors chose to go on and do more than the appropriation called for, they could do so under the contract.
What was that contract for?
For dredging. There was another contract on the 4th of June last. They had a right under the contract, if they chose to employ dredges enough, to do the whole work this year.
About how much would that have amounted to?

Probably two or three million dollars. This work, proceeding with ordinary rapidity, would run over three or four years Then there is an amount of $31,000 to pay Mr. Hogan. That is under an old contract made in 1906.
How much was voted last year on the Hogan contract?

The vote was a lump sum of $600,000 for improvements at Port Arthur, which included dredging and the breakwater. I say frankly to the committee that when, during last summer, our revenues began to improve, I felt that I would not be doing my duty to the country, in view of the rapid development of the country and the necessity of providing as soon as possible the requisite accommodation, if I had said to these people, who had contracts and who were entitled to go on and do the work, though they might have to wait until parliament had voted the money to pay for it, 'You must stop work.' On the other hand, I allowed them to go on, and I believe parliament will ratify what was done and provide the money this vear, instead of compelling the contractors to wait until next year. Of course, there is the question of interest, but it was much better we allowed them to go ahead with the work and now pay them, and so close up the account for the year.

I think that the principle laid down by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is perfectly correct. Parliament is called once a year to vote money to be expended on public works and other necessities of administration. Parliament granted $600,000 for this work and the minister spent $425,000 more than we voted. That over expenditure was an open violation of the first principles of responsible government. Why this farce of our coming here to vote Mr. PUGSLEY.
these expenditures at all if the ministers can afterwards spend as much money as they like regardless of our vote. This is a matter which should engage the attention of every member of parliament, because it strikes at the very root of parliamentary authority. Let the minister of any department go on spending 80 or 90 per cent more than the amount we authorized him to spend, and what becomes of parliamentary control? If we go through the different items, I have no doubt that we will find many millions of dollars spent without any parliamentary vote. It seems to me that we ought not for a moment to sanction anything of the kind. We ought at least to stick to first principles and see that no money is expended unless authorized by parliament except in some very extreme and unforeseen emergencies.

I was not here when this discussion began, but as I understand something about the work done up there, perhaps a word from me, as an independent outsider, will show that there are certain mitigating circumstances in this case. Fort William and Port Arthur are two great harbours of Ontario, and certain works were planned to be done at these harbours extending over many years. Parliament votes a certain amount for these works every year, and, as I understand, the work has been anticipated. But if the minister can have the work done in two years instead of four, I think the country will gain by having that much earlier the use of the harbours and those improvements. If these works could all be done in one year, that would be still a greater benefit. The trade has grown so enormously that the facilities at Fort William and Port Arthur are altogether inadequate, and if the business continues to grow, any delay in the prosecution of the government works will cause great injury to shippers at the head of the lake.

What would the observations of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) lead to if they were made generally applicable? Last year we voted altogether $100,000,000. Out of that amount we voted for Port Arthur and Fort William $600,000, but we spent during the year $1,025,000, or we spent nearly $2 for every one that parliament voted. Surely that extra expenditure was not expenditure which could not have been foreseen with the exercise of a little good judgment and foresight. Surely parliament should have been asked to vote that money before it was expended. Suppose the same principle were carried out all along the line and that our revenue had fallen off, and suppose we found ourselves at the end of the year with an expenditure of $200,000,000 when we had only voted $100,000,000, what

would then be the financial- condition of the country. I am not objecting to any reasonable expenditure, but 1 am objecting to such excessive expenditure not authorized by parliament. When we find a minister spending two dollars for every one we voted, it is time that parliament should express in no doubtful terms its condemnation of such conduct. It is a violation of the principle of constitutional government.
If that be so, how is it that every year since confederation we have voted supplementary estimates for the current year?
We vote them before the money is expended.
No, we vote them to pay the debts due on the 31st March, which were not provided for by parliamentary sanction.

In some cases that is done, but only in exceptional cases It is done to meet expenditures which could not have been anticipated at the time the estimates were brought down, but which had to be incurred owing to urgent need. But that is not the case here. In this case parliament voted the money which the government asked for, parliament in so doing exercised its judgment and understood that the vote should not be exceeded, but here we have the minister spending two dollars for every one voted, and then asking parliament to condone his conduct by voting money to meet the deficiency. This is not a case of a sudden and unforeseen emergency. Such a case as that would justify the expenditure.
For such cases you get a Governor General's warrant.

They may be provided for by Governor General's warrant or otherwise, and parliament will overlook a great deal in consideration of the circumstances; but in such a case as this, any intelligent engineer should have known what amount would be required and have furnished an estimate for that amount. How many more dredges did they put on during the year than they expected to put on at the beginning?
One very powerful suction dredge which they bought for that purpose.	.
How many more have they?
Five more.

Where a contract has been made, and it is expected that certain amount of work will be done during the year, and parliament has voted the money,
if the amount were over-run a little, parliament would not object to that. But it is carrying it too far, and is defying the fundamental principles of parliamentary government when very large expenditures are made, and then the minister comes in an unconcerned, commonplace way, and says: The money is spent, and it will have to be voted. Suppose every minister did the same thing, is it not easy to see to what abuses it would lead? The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has acquired the reputation of being very strong-willed, and of taking his own way, whether right or wrong, doing what he feels disposed to do regardless of parliament. Both the House, and the country are taking note of this. The hon. minister may carry this out to a limited extent, but a day of retribution will come when the public disapproval will be visited upon him and hi3 colleagues, for an abuse that ought not to be tolerated by parliament.

I quite agree that the government ought not to engage in any work not authorized by parliament. But parliament has over and over again sanctioned this great work at Port Arthur and Fort William; parliament has been fully informed of the expenditure from year to year. The work has been carried on according to a design prepared by the engineers in conjunction with the railway companies which are making their termini at Fort William and Port Arthur. Parliament has been informed, substantially, what this is going to cost. Therefore, this puts the present case entirely aside from the cases to which the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) has referred, of the government engaging in new work without the sanction of parliament.
Is not the dredging of the Grand Trunk Pacific harbour new work ?
No. How in the world can you develop a harbour on Mission river unless you have a turning basin?
Why did not the minister ask for the money for that if he knew it was to be done?
Let me tell the hon. member what occurred. Early in the year, Mr. Chamberlin, of the Grand Trunk Pacific, said to me: 'We expect to take part in moving the crops this year
About what time was this?

May or June. He said they expected to move the crops over their road by October 1. The line was to be finished from Edmonton to Winnipeg, and also the branch from Lake Superior Junction to Fort William, and they were informed by the commissioners of the Trans-

continental that their part of the work necessary for this purpose would be finished. He represented that it would be most unfortunate if the Grand Trunk Pacific could not utilize its elevator at Fort William, and the only way by which it could be utilized would be by dredging the channel-I think about half a mile-between the Mission river and the elevator. I told Mr. Chamberlin that I did not know that 1 could do this, as it might cost more money than the government could afford to spend that year. He urged upon me that it would be a most deplorable thing if, by reason of the delay of the government in this dredging work, the Grand Trunk Pacific was not able to handle the crop of 1909. I brought the matter before my colleagues, especially Sir Richard Cartwright, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who keeps in touch more especially with the trade of the country. I found he was strongly impressed with the rapidity with which the trade there was developing, and with the importance of doing everything we reasonably could to give the requisite facilities at Port Arthur and Fort William. I sent for the contractor, and was informed by one of the gentlemen in charge of the contracting work that it would be utterly impossible for them to make the connection between Mission river and the elevator by dredging the channel-because it was an entirely new channel-unless they purchased a very powerful suction dredge, and they could only get such a dredge in the United States. I conferred again with my colleagues, presenting the whole matter to them, and they concurred in the view that in these pressing and urgent circumstances, if the contractor could, by bringing in an additional dredge, accomplish what the Grand Trunk Pacific desired, and what seemed to be in the interest of the whole country, and especially of the west, should be accomplished of having this route opened for traffic by the 1st of October, it was desirable to allow the dredging contractors to put another dredge upon the work. With that encouragement they went to the United States, bought a powerful suction dredge, brought it in, paid the duties on it, and put it at work. And, with this dredge and the others they have a very large plant of six different dredges. They were able to dredge out the channel, and make a connection with the elevator so that steamers could go from the Mission river to the elevator. We did our work, and did it in anticipation of it being necessary for the companies to handle the grain in time for that season, and I am proud that our department did this work on time, and accomplished what we assured the Grand Trunk Pacific would be done. But it was only by the contractor putting forth additional effort, and buy-Mr. PUGSLEY.
ing this extra plant that the work was accomplished. The hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule), says:	Suppose the
revenues had declined? In that case I doubt very much if we should have allowed the work to go on as we did. We should probably have said to the contractors: ' You will have to stop work on the Grand Trunk Pacific elevator channel, for, much as we desire to give connection to that elevator this season yet, in the state of the revenues, we do not think it desirable in the public interest to go ahead. But the revenues began to improve and remained buoyant, so I took the responsibility of ordering this work, in connection with my colleagues, and particularly with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir Richard Cartwright, than whom there is no more prudent man in the country. I think parliament should say we have done the right thing. It makes no difference whether we provide for the work now or next year, or last year. For it must be borne in mind that these contractors had a contract for an area-not for a season, but for the entire work-and they were entitled to proceed with it as rapidly as they chose, but always subject to their being allowed to wait until parliament should appropriate the money to make the payment. It is, as the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. [DOT]T. A. Currie) has said to the committee. If a public work involved an expenditure of $1,000,000,, if it were in the hands of a contractor who was expected to finish $500,000 of the work in a season would there be any quarrel with him because he does building to the extent of $750,000? The contractor puts on a large force of men, employs the best of machinery, and gets along with the buildipg to the extent of $750,000. Is there any violation of the principle of responsible government in allowing him to do that? Is there any encroachment on the law of parliament? It would be my duty as minister to say to parliament that the contractor had gone on more rapidly than we expected, and I am sure parliament would cheerfully grant the necessary money to pay him. It is exactly the same in this case. Parliament had given its sanction to the full performance of these contracts.

The member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is perfectly correct in what he said. The Minister of Public Works has gone the wrong way about getting his money. If he had had this statement in the main estimates for next year it could have been included in the Supply Bill which was passed the other day and the money would have been available sooner than it will be in this way because it will now be impossible to include this in a Supply Bill before the first of April. If he had asked for this money

in that way there -would have been no question about it.

I agree with the principle advanced by the members tor Grey and Kings, Prince Edward Island. We are here to decide on how we shall spend so many millions of dollars. We 'have so many millions at our disposal and according to the judgment of the House the money is divided and expended in different parts of the country for necessary public works. If going over these estimates means anything it means that they are submitted to the judgment of the House and the money is divided according to the best judgment of the majority of the members. The principle laid down by the minister to-night is in effect that if after the supplies are granted the revenues increase, he as Minister of Public Works has a perfect right to expend the increased revenue without applying to or getting the sanction of parliament for the expenditure.
I did not say that, I said that I might be justified in allowing a contractor to proceed with his work more rapidly.

It is not a question ot whether this work is necessary at Fort William and Port Arthur; W'e will grant that it is, and that much more money should be expended there. The question is whether a minister should take it upon himself after the money of the country has been divided, to sepnd hundreds of thousands of dollars without receiving the sanction of parliament. For instance, last year I asked the minister to spend a few hundred dollars in my riding, but he told me the money had been expended and that there was no money available for that particular work. He did not say it was unnecessary or not in the interests of the people. I contend that in the expenditure of this money I have the right, as any member has, to lay the claims of mv county for a fair share of this money before this House, and to let the judgment of the House say whether or not that money should be expended. I object to the principle of a minister of the Crown taking it upon himself to expend several hundred thousand dollars for a work no matter how necessary it may be without having received the sanction of parliament. The minister has referred to the erecting of a public building to cost $2,000,000 and argues that he would be justified in going beyond the appropriation for a certain year if the contractor had gone beyond the amount voted. I do not think that could be done without infringing on the rights of other parts of the country to a fair share of the money. While I believe it is very necessary to have this work done, I wish to
put myself on record as being opposed on principle to a minister expending some $400,000 more than the amount to which this House gave its sanction.

The minister has neglected to state that a commission sat on this harbour and decided to make it a national harbour and that plans for that purpose were adopted. The Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway adjusted their plans to the plans adopted by the government. That report was presented to the House and is to be found among our sessional papers. The government is carrying on that work and the Grand Trunk Pacific has certainlv opened up a large extent of territory which must be served. That road reached completion at Fort-William much more rapidly than the government anticipated. I was there a year ago last fall and I concluded that the Grand Trunk Pacific would have to wait with their elevator at least a year before they could get a boat to it. I am pleased that the government has rushed the work. Private money to the extent of $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 is invested in the elevator, and it would not be fair to have a couple of millions stand idle for a year or two years owing to the slowness of the government work. I am pleased that the minister has decided to rush the work, because there is a great deal more work necessary to complete the harbour. If the minister had directed the contractor last year to stop the work owing to lack of money voted by parliament so that the elevator would have had to stand idle, I am afraid that the whole northwest would have been here tearing his head off for causing that delay. If this money were being expended on a worthless or political job, then I would say that the member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) was quite right and that it should not be done, but this is a national work, one of our greatest national works in transportation. I cannot see that the minister has done very much wrong in doing what he has done.

The hon. member for North Sim-coe (Mr. Currie) can become as much of an apologist as he likes for the minister's conduct, but that will not influence my action in this House one iota. The hon. member gives the very strongest reason why parliament -should have been asked for this expenditure last year -When he says that the commission visited that harbour and decided to make a certain report and that that report was made and presented to parliament last year. Therefore, they must have been in possession of that report, they must have known what was required to be done, and they should have submitted the estimate to parliament.
I did not say that the report was presented last year. The report was presented two years ago, and the work has been carried on by this government for three years in accordance with that report.

That makes it so much the worse, and it makes my -argument stronger because it was known the longer beforehand. I am not objecting to any expenditure at Port Arthur, per se, because it is a very important harbour, and if twice as large an expenditure had been proposed last session -as was proposed, I have not the slightest doubt that this House would have voted it. But, I object to the principle. I say it is unparliamentary and wrong notwithstanding anything that has been said by the Minister of Public Works or ^he hon. member for North Simcoe. I am not very much concerned in either case. The hon. member for North Simcoe has asked:	What would the Northwest have
said if they could not have got their grain down there and through the elevator if it had been ready to receive it? We were told last session that the- Grand Trunk Pacific would be hauling the crop of 1909 down to Port Arthur. Then, if they were going to haul grain, if it were known beforehand and we had that information given to this House by the ministers of the Crown, what kind of business men must they be, knowing that, that they did not prepare for it in proper time? If there h-ad been provision in the proper time, this Hou-se could have authorized the expenditure and the harbour could have been made ready for navigation in time to permit the Grand Trunk Pacific to handle that grain. The minister said that the president of the railway company came to him last May or June. Does he not remember that this House only adjourned on the 19th -or 20th of May? If it were in May surely- he could have tol-d this House w-hat was needed, and this House would have willingly voted it. But they came to the minister a few weeks after parliament rose. How did it happen that it was known a few weeks after parliament rose and it was not known a few weeks before? All these plans are not the result of a moment's excitement. They are all worked out beforehand. They have to look over the ground, provide -and prepare months beforehand. Therefore, it was known, the company had their consultations with the government, no doubt, and the government engineers had gone into the question and determined the amount of work which was required to be done, -and the depth of dredging necessary to enable them to ship through these elevators. That was all known beforehand, and therefore I think that this expenditure ought to have been provided for by parliament. I am not -objecting to the expenditure. If it Mr. SPROTJLE.
had been ten times as much I would not object because I know' the importance of that harbour, but I am objecting to the unparliamentary principle that has been adopted and has been introduced by the Minister of Public Works, one which parliament should not condone and one which parliament should not allow to pass.
It was- not introduced by me. I am following what has been done for forty years.
Not by any means. A few thousand dollars here and there-
But on the same principle.

For every dollar that parliament has voted you -spend $1.75 during the year on this work. We voted $600,000 and you spend $1,025,000. Yet, we are told that such a principle is defensible. No such principle that I have any knowledge of in parliamentary life is defensible. I have said all I intend to say about it, but I say that the government and the Minister of Public Works ought to be held responsible and called to account for it by the people of this country.

I have no objection to the item as fax as this harbour is concerned. I know very little about the merits of the question, but there is a principle recognized by the people of this country. One thing that we are assembled in parliament for is to look after the expenditure of public money. The principle of the -appropriation of public money is one which is recognized by every banking or financial institution to-day in Canada. It is a well recognized principle that all moneys that axe to be expended -shall be voted by a Board of Directors, or, as in the case of public money, by this parliament. The principle is the same. Last year the Minister of Public Work-s asked for $600,000 to expend on this public work. It was granted. A few months afterwards a man by the name of Chamberlin, a contractor up there, the president of some company, comes to the minister-
He is the manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Well, he comes to the minister and tells him that he wants more' money to be granted. This is shortly after parliament closed, or perhaps before parliament closed. The minister says: Yes, we will get at the thing and we will spend $400,000 more. For what purpose? So that we may be able to get the grain out. What do the Grand Trunk Pacific do? They take out one train load of grain. The minister has departed from a fundamental principle of constitutional government.

Although this may be, as the hon. member for North Simcoe says, a necessary work, surely this parliament will try and govern itself in accordance with fundamental principles. If we are going to get away from them why come and ask for any more money for this work? Let them go on and spend the money, and at the end of the year come and tell us how much they have expended. Why do they go through the farce of coming and asking parliament for $600,000 when at the end of the year they will come back and tell us that they have spent over a million dollars? I feel sure that if we go over the different items in the accounts for the year we will find expenditures without the authorization of parliament amounting to thousands and even millions of dollars a year. What business has the minister or any department of the government to spend a million dollars without the authorization of parliament? Surely it is the duty of parliament to authorize public expenditures, and I think every lion, member will concede that it is a principle and a duty that should be adhered to.

I would like to ask the minister whether the place that is being dredged by the suction dredge is not likely to fill in again with material washed from the lake or the river. I want to call his attention to what I think is the most serious part of this whole question. I think my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is perfectly right in criticising the minister for this large expenditure of money without the consent of parliament. The minister quoted to us the amount of the expenditure on each of the contracts let previous to the present year, and these contracts, as I added them up, amount to only $350,000, which leaves $75,000 of new contracts that the minister has let on his own responsibility. To my mind that is the most serious part of the whole transaction.
Did my hon. friend take the $55,000 paid to the Great Lakes Dredging Company for the deepening of the river from 22 to 25 feet?
I understood the minister to make the statement that there was a contract for $55,000.
Yes, that was for deepening the channel from 22 to 25 feet. That is part of the same work.
Is that not a new contract?
It is new instructions, but still that would be included in the work originally designed.
Did it cost the same?
It cost a little more to go to the greater depth.
Well, it must be a new contract.
It was not a new work. It is all part of the one harbour.
How much more per yard is paid to the Great Lakes Dredging Company for this deeper work than for the other?

A part of it had already been dredged to 22 feet, and then we had to provide for the extra 3 feet, and where it had not been dredged at all, we dredged down to 25 feet, and the whole thing was figured out with very great care by the engineers. I cannot give the figures exactly, but I think we raised it from 9 cents for the 22 feet to 111 cents for the 25 feet, which is a very reasonable figure.
How much was earned by the Great Lakes Dredging Company last year?
I will get the information on the main estimates.
New work for at least $75,000, including the deepening of the harbour, was let last year.

The only really new work was the $10,000 worth done by Mr. Phinn.
Tiffin harbour improvements, $23,000.

This is to provide for amount due contractors for drilling and dredging operations at Tiffin to a depth of 25 feet at low ivater in connection with the terminals of the Grand Trunk. The important harbour at Tiffin is part of the national system of transportation, and we have decided to dredge there to 25 feet.
How much w!as voted, last year?
$125,000, and ive have expended $147,377.88.
Does that complete the work?
No, we will continue work this year.

How much has been spent on this harbour, and how much i3 yet to be expended?
Mr, PUGSLEY. We have already expended $384,000 at Tiffin, and the engineer tells me the total estimated cost will be $600,000.

Victoria harbour improvements, $36,000.
We had an appropriation last year of $150,000, and we have expended $185,526.
Will the minister have sufficient depth of water for the Canadian Pacific railway at these elevators?
Yes; the Canadian Pacific railway is entirely satisfied with the way in which the work is proceeding.
You should take enough money this year, so that we may not have the same complication we have had over Fort William. There is a lot of work to be done at Victoria harbour.
I think we are taking enough money.
Is that work let by contract?

It is under contract, let after public advertisement for tenders; rock, $2.25 a yard; other materials, 124 cents w'hen towed; boulders, $1.75; all other materials, 11 cents per cubic yard when cast over.
The whole contract is let to one company?
Yes.
What is the total estimated cost?
I think it will be more.
Perhaps a little more. In reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) I may say we have the usual slope, and it is rather hard material there, so that it is not likely to fill in to any extent.
The banks and the bottom of the river are heavy red clay.
Then why have you to pay for rock cutting?

There is some hard granite rock there.
Further amount required towards the encouragement of better transportation and conservation of fresh fish, $20,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The reason for this supplementary vote is that this service has proved itself so effective in the development of the fresh fish trade that it was decided to continue it through the fiscal year. The whole explanation of the arrangement covers two and a half pages of the last report of the Fisheries Department, beginning at page 17. The policy of the department has been to guarantee one-third of the ordinary express rates to Quebec and Ontario in order to encourage the direct Mr. PUGSLEY.
shipment of fresh fish. Formerly it came to Montreal via Boston.
How much was voted forjhis purpose last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: $25,000. That was to carry on the work to November last, but it has proven so successful that the department decided to continue it, and the additional $20,000 is required to meet the additional expense. The ordinary express rates from Port Mulgrave or Halifax to Montreal is $1.50 per hundred pounds. Of that we pay fifty cents, so that it costs $1 per hundred pounds to cover the shipment to Montreal.

I do not want to be understood as opposing this, because I think that anything that will tend to stimulate trade between the various provinces is very desirable, but I am afraid that the minister would get into trouble if he attempted to apply the same rule to all other commodities.
We have been doing that for a long time for butter, cheese and fruit.
Not paying one-third of the express rates.

We have been doing it in a different form. We have been guaranteeing to the railway companies that they would earn two-thirds of the ordinary freight rates per car. If they do not get enough freight in the car to earn two-thirds, we make up the difference. If they get more than two-third3, they give us a credit for the extra, and at the end of the season a balance is struck, and we make up the loss. We spend about $10,000 a year on that.

I think there is a great constitutional principle at stake here. I quite agree that it is a good thing to encourage the shipment of fresh fish from the maritime provinces as far as Montreal, and to pay part of the freight on it, to the province of Ontario, where it may compete with the fish caught by our fishermen on the great lakes; but I notice that when there is any expenditure for the province of Ontario every one seems to want to jump on it with both feet. I do not believe in being provincial in this matter; but the mistake made in this case is the same as in the case of the Minister of Public Works, that the money was expended without the consent of parliament.

I understand that this is a sort of bonus given for the purpose of driving the American fish out of our market. This market was formerly supplied by the Boston dealers, and it was to enable our Canadians to compete with the Boston men that this money is given.

I think the object very commendable and I presume the increase is due to the development of the trade. In place of voting the $30,000 in the estimate last year, that vote ought to be increased.

There is a great constitutional principle at stake right here again and, as representing an Ontario constituency, I say -we ought to come right back to that principle. The minister has Violated a constitutional principle by overrunning this estimate, what would he do if he had to spend a million dollars? No doubt he would overrun it bv $500.-
000.

Why should not the fishermen on the north shore of Lake Superior have some of the benefits of this? They are nearly as far from the Montreal market as the deep ^ea fishermen and they have to express their fish.
They do not compete with the American fish.
Yes, they do. They ship white trout and pickerel.

And the fishermen of Lake Manitoba, represented bv the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), catch two million to three million dollars worth of fish every year and ship them to the United States. Why should they not have a share in this money? But again I would remind the House that there is a great constitutional principle at stake, and I hope my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) will support me in'opposing this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The policy has been to give assistance to salt water fishermen only.

Why?
_ Mr. TEMPLEMAN. The policy was only inaugurated one or two years ago and the idea was to bring the Atlantic fisheries into Ontario and Quebec.
Thev have Spain and Cuba and other countries to shin to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I frankly admit that if the principle is sound in one case, it ought to be in another, and I would advise the department to consider the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee). Just to show the effect of this, take the imports from the United States into the port of Montreal, _ the greatest Canadian fish market. The importation of such fish as cod and haddock from the United States fell in 1898 to the end of October from 753,000 pounds to 75,000 pounds in the case of cod and from 75,000 of haddock to 9,000 pounds.
182J
This shows that the American fish had been displaced by direct importation from the Atlantic.

I might reply to the observations of the hon. member	for
North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that this is not a matter to turn into a jest. The principle in the present instance is entirely different from that in the case we discussed some time ago. Some years ago we passed a law to give certain consideration to those who shipped butter, cheese or other perishable produce in cold storage, and we voted $75,000 for that purpose, but it was distinctly understood that if the trade cailed	for
more we would give more in the same proportion. In the case before us the principle is just the same. It it were decided to give for this article of produce one-third of the cost of transportation and it was assumed so many tons would be shipped, and the shipments happened to exceed that amount, there is no violation of principle in paying the extra percentage. That is not the same at all as an over expenditure on a public work. In the latter case, the engineers have every opportunity of drawing plans and making estimates and submitting everything to parliament, and there can be no excuse for the minister doubling the expenditure voted.
Does the Minister of Agriculture provide cold storage facilities for shipment of butter in the winter?
No.
Cold storage was supplied for the fish business in the summer, but now the minister asks an additional appropriation during the winter. Again there is a great constitutional principle at stake.
On butter in winter we do not need cold storage.
Nor do we need it on fish.

The fish is expressed and not sent in cold storage at all.
Fish breeding establishments-amount required to pay AY. S. Young for special service collecting whitefish eggs for hatchery at Selkirk and Berens river, $100.

I have thought for a good many years that the government are not doing all they should with regard to the establishment of these fish hatcheries. The rivers and lakes of our country are being depleted very rapidly. In the Georgian bay we have one of the very finest fishing grounds in Canada, but it is being rapidly depleted. Every year immense quantities of fish and fish ova are brought
[DOT]5751

to the shore and the fish ova -destroyed, in some places in tons, and yet we require them. The Americans take them. and use them for hatching out fish on their side. Instead of having those fish ova destroyed, as they are in some cases in tons, we would be doing the proper thing if more fish breeding establishments were erected on the Georgian bay and Lake Huron, and have the fish hatched out there. They send to Georgian bay and collect the ova there right along the shore of the riding I represent. They bring them to Ottawa and hatch them out, and afterwards the fresh fry are taken back at considerable expense and put into the lake. The hatching might as well be done there at the edge of the lake, in the streams that are in every way suitable for the purpose. Many of the fry are destroyed in carriage, and it costs a good deal 'more while yielding nothing like the beneficial results that would follow having hatcheries near the water in which the fry are to be placed. I have again and again drawn attention to this improper and short-sighted policy. For some time I thought I had the promise of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that he would establish a hatchery on the river leading into Thornbury down through a portion of my riding, where there are opportunities for a dozen fish hatcheries close to the lake. Though I thought I had his promise, I found that the minister was only jollying the thing along, and I was forced to the conclusion that he had no intention of carrying out the idea. I understand that one hatchery was established at Wiarton. That is right. I would like to see a dozen along the Georgian bay including one at Southampton. Tons of fish ova are destroyed there every year, and the waters are being depleted and the public are complaining. We are talking of conserving our forests and of replanting. That is what we should do with our fisheries; we should make the best use of all that nature has given us.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am inclined to agree with the observations of my bon. friend (Mr. Sprouleb Not many hatcheries have been built in very recent years. I am informed that it is proposed to build one on Lake Superior, and two or three applications for hatcheries on Georgian bay, and other points along that lake shore are under consideration at present.
Is one on the Beaver river?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am informed that that is not one of those under consideration. I believe that the view expressed by my hon. friend has the concurrence of the department which has always been anxious to establish fish hatcheries. There are

thirty-seven hatcheries in Canada, and, of these fully two-thirds have been established within the last ten years. In my own province there are nine, eight of which have been built within the last ten or twelve years. We are well supplied in British Columbia for the hatching of salmon. The policy of the department has always been to build hatcheries, and keep up the fisheries by this artificial propagation. If I can influence the department, I will try to have others built on the great lakes.
Is it the intention to hatch shad at the Windsor hatchery?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am advised that that is being provided for, that provision is being made in the main estimates in relation to that matter.
Fisheries protection service-further amount required, $30,000.
What protection service is this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is to provide for expenditures of last year. This vote is necessary largely because of additional fisheries protection on the Pacific ocean. The protection of the sea fisheries there is a verv serious question. The government has had only one cruiser, the ' Kestrel.' It was felt that another vessel was needed, and the steamer ' Joliffe,' a large and powerful tug was engaged in the service at an expense of $9,000 or $10,000. Another large item covered by this vote is repairs to the government cruiser ' Kestrel.' No repairs of any account had been made to this vessel since she was built in 1903. An examination showed serious defects and she was put on the wavs and thoroughly repaired at a cost of $13,000.

Will the minister be good enough to tell us where the bulk of this money is expended?

It is chiefly in the western provinces, on the new railway systems, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. I know of forty or fifty post offices on these lines that were established two or three years ago. At the beginning the receipts were $25, or $30, or $40. I remember that the best revenue producing office was Wainwright, one of the divisional points on the Grand Trunk Pacific. The revenue was then about $175; now it has increased to nearly $1,000. It shows the progress of the country in these new sections. New settlements grow up and new offices are opened. That is where the great bulk of the business is done now, but in the older sections of the country we are establishing post offices, reducing the distances between offices and giving better postal facilities.

I see the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Conedon) sitting behind the minister, and I was wondering whether he was asking for an expenditure for increased postal facilities in that part of the country. I see that last year there was an expenditure of $135,000 in the Yukon.

We have to contend with special circumstances in the Yukon. It is not a profitable business on account of the prives that have to be paid for the services, and the distances covered to reach the mining camps that are dispersed throughout that land. It is not a profitable business, but still we have to maintain the service. We have to be in a position to send a letter from north to south or east to west at two cents. We take pride in the Post Office Department in the fact that persons at the remotest points in this country can send and receive letters. As an instance of the development of postal facilities in the west. I may say that since 1908 we have established in the district of Medicine Hat alone, something like 60 offices. It shows the rapid development that is taking place in the west, and how difficult it is to predict in advance the amount that will be spent in a year. That is why I am obliged to come now and ask for an additional vote of $200,000.

To provide for the appointment of R. G. Meroer as superintendent of the railway mail service at London, at a salary of $1,500 a year from the 1st April, 1909, $1,500.
Is that a new aopoint-ment?

No, he succeeds another gentleman. Mr. Mercer has been employed since 1872, first in the inspector's office, and then in the office of the Superintendent of Railway Mail Service. On the death of the late superintendent, in July, 1905, Mr. Mercer was placed in charge of the district, and has given very good satisfaction. He is known as a first-class clerk, and he is now in receipt of the maximum salary of $1,500. Under the statute, however, no person can be appointed as superintendent unless he has actually been employed as a railway mail clerk for two and a half years. Mr. Mercer has never been employed in that capacity, and, therefore, his appointment has to be made by a vote in the estimates.
Then you are deliberately and flagrantly defying the Civil Service Act?
He is now at his maximum, and we simplv propose to change his title, he continuing to receive the same salary. He has been acting since 1905.
In that capacity?
Yes, but he had not the title.

I understand the minister to say that the law provides that a man occupying the position of superintendent must be employed two and a half years. If he was there since 1905, he must have been employed more than two and a half years. The minister must be wrong in his explanation. I take it that the salary is being voted because he has not complied with the Act.

I do not know the details of the situation enough to be able to explain them, but under the new Civil Service Act a salary of this kind cannot be voted unless a man's name is put into the item, and I think that is the reason of this particular item. The amount may have been provided and paid otherwise, but the item must contain the name according to the provision of the Civil Service Act.
I want to call the attention of the minister for a moment to some communications I have received in reference to ' Cotton's Weekly,' published at Cowansville.
Is my hon. friend a socialist?
That is not to the point.
Not at all.

I do not need to_ be a socialist in order to wish to do justice. I know not whether injustice has been done in this matter, but I am requested by some of my constituents to call the attention of the Postmaster General to what is alleged to be a grievance. I have a letter from Mr. McQuarrie, a gentleman in the town of Barrie who is an avowed socialist, but a man whom I hold in the very highest esteem. I have also a petition from some people who live very close to me in the little hamlet where I reside, and they represent that an injustice has been done. I shall send that petition to the Postmaster General. Now, I do not know whether this is a good publication or not, but my correspondents allege that discrimination has been practised against them. I see in a copy which has been addressed to me as well as other members, a letter addressed to the Postmaster General complaining that by a recent order the postmaster at Cowansville has charged sixteen times the amount formerly charged as postage on this publication. If this is an improper publication which should not have the privilege to go through the mails it should be shut out altogether, but if it is entitled to postal privileges it ought not to be charged more than the rates charged other publications. As a public man representing these people who have communicated with me; I want to bring the matter squarely before the Postmaster General, and to ask him for an explanation.

I have had communications similar to those received by my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) and I endorse the statements made by him. If this publication is not such as should pass through the post office, it should be stopped altogether, but if it is entitled to postal privileges it should be treated the same as any other newspaper. I ask, for those interested in this paper, fair and reasonable and impartial treatment.
When I made a remark to my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) a moment ago, of course, he understood it was a joke.
Oh, certainly, I did not resent it at all.

It is quite proper that my hon. friend should ask the reason for the complaints made by Mr. Cotton, the editor of ' Cotton's Weekly '. I have been deluged with letters from all parts of the country, not only from those who believe in

socialistic doctrines, but from other citizens, who want to see fair play done to every section of the community. I must say at once that there has been no discrimination,	whatever, against ' Cotton's
Weekly	If there was anything published
in that paper of a scurrilous character' it would be prevented altogether from passing through the mails, as has been done in other cases, but ' Cotton's Weekly ' is not a paper of that class. Through an error of the postmaster as Cowansville, where the paper is published, it was allowed to pass through the mails in bundles, paying the same rate as if the paper had been addressed to bona fide subscribers. There is a postal rate for bona fide subscribers, and there is a certain other rate charged for papers sent in bundles. As soon as the attention of the department was called to that fact the proper legal rate was exacted from the publishers, and hence all the trouble. I repeat that there is no discrimination, whatever. Mr. Cotton is under the impression that we are discriminating against his paper, because it is a socialistic paper, but the department has no idea of the kind in mind. The fact is that Mr. Cotton is sending his paper in bundles to certain individuals, who then distribute them to other parties.
They are not individually addressed?

They are not individually addressed. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) is a distinguished member of the bar, and he knows the legal definition of ' bona fide subscribers ' used in this sense. The whole thing in a nut-shell is that Mr. Cotton addresses his papers in bundles to one individual, who then distributes, or sells, them to others, and that does not mean a ' bona fide subscriber ' as set out in the Postal Act. There have been hundreds of complaints sent to me that there is an attempt by the Post Office Department to crush this paper because of its socialistic character, and I have answered every one of these correspondents, explaining the matter very fully. There is no discrimination in the Post Office Department against any respectable opinion which may be advanced by any citizens. I respect the views of the socialists, I respect the views of the labour people as I respect the views of all classes of the community, and I would not be a party to lending the authority of the post office to suppress any respectable opinion. Mr. Cotton is completely in error about this. He has written to his friends throughout the country telling them to write to the Post Office Department to state that we are trying to destroy his paper. Such is not the case. We are simply charging him the rate which is charged in every other similar case. The other day I gave more, in reply to a question, the legal aspect of the matter, which will be found in ' Hansard '.

Do I understand the Postmaster General to say that the rate imposed upon ' Cotton's Weekly ' at Cowansville, in bundles without individual addresses, is exactly the same rate that would be charged to any other weekly paper issuing from the same place, whatever its opinions might be?
That is correct.
Then, if they were addressed to bona fide subscribers and put into a bundle, they would be allowed to go at a lower rate?
Yes.
And it was because this was detected, and they had been allowed to go at a rate which they should not have gone that the change was made?
Yes.
The Postmaster General says that he has answered a great many letters. Has he answered Mr. Cotton?

Mr. Cotton wrote me yesterday a personal letter, in which I am sorry to say he abused me terribly; but I ignored the abuse and answered the facts. I signed the letter this afternoon. He labours under the delusion that he is discriminated against, whereas the department is simply treating him as it does any other editor in the country.

While this item is under discussion I would like to call the Postmaster General's attention to the mail service in the Paroy Sound district. We have certain new lines of railway in that district, and yet in a great many cases the people continue to get their mails by the old routes^ perhaps by a vehicle carrying it fifteen miles when there is a railroad within a mile or two. I think it would be advisable for the Postmaster General to have the inspector make an inquiry into the service and report.

I shall be pleased to give the railroads the preference in every case, and I may say to my hon. friend that when a railroad is completed, the company does not lose any time in coming to the department and asking for the privilege of transporting His. Majesty's mail. However, if my hon. friend will call my attention to any railway company which has no transportation of the mails, I will have the matter looked into.

I may cite a case in point. There is a town in my county called

Byng Inlet to which there is a mail service north by the Canadian Pacific railway, I think, on alternate days. There is no return service south, and a letter from Byng Inlet to Parry Sound goes north to Sudbury, from there to North Bay, from there to Toronto, and back again to Parry Sound. In that way it takes six or seven days for the letter to reach its destination, whereas a man could walk down the track and deliver the letter in a few hours. That is one ease, but there are a great many others, and I think it would be well for the minister to have the inspector look into the whole mail service of that district.
